questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Vector Equation of a Line Given in Canonical Form
questions.problem: Consider the straight line with the canonical equation $\frac{x-3}{5}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z+7}{-5}.$ Find the vector equation of the line.
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$, is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Comparing the above to our given equation

$$
\frac{x-3}{5}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z-(-7)}{-5},
$$

we find that our line passes through the point $P(3,1,-7)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨5,1,-5⟩.$ Therefore, its vector equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -7\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line Given in Parametric or Vector Form
questions.problem:
Consider the straight line with the vector equation

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
questions.worked_solution:
We have the vector equation 

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

This implies that the straight line passes through the point $P(1,-2,3)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨4,3,-1⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-1}{4}=\frac{y-(-2)}{3}=\frac{z-3}{-1}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x-1}{4}=\frac{y+2}{3}=\frac{z-3}{-1}.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the straight line with the parametric equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=3-2t \\ y=-5t \\ z=1-t\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3-2t \\ -5t \\ 1-t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2t \\ -5t \\ -t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -5 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -5 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

This implies that the given line passes through the point $P(3,0,1)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨-2,-5,-1⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-3}{-2}=\frac{y-0}{-5}=\frac{z-1}{-1}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x-3}{-2}=\frac{y}{-5}=\frac{z-1}{-1}.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the straight line with the parametric equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=2-6t \\ y=1+3t \\ z=-5+2t\end{aligned}
$$

 
for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2-6t \\ 1+3t \\ -5+2t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-6t \\ 3t \\ 2t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

This implies that the straight line passes through the point $P(2,1,-5)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨-6,3,2⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-2}{-6}=\frac{y-1}{3}=\frac{z-(-5)}{2}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x-2}{-6}=\frac{y-1}{3}=\frac{z+5}{2}.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -9 \\ 11\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-7}{-3}=\frac{y-(-9)}{2}=\frac{z-11}{0}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x-7}{-3}=\frac{y+9}{2}=\frac{z-11}{0},
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{z-11}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $z$ component always maintains the constant value of $z=11:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}7-3t \\ -9+2t \\ 11\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{z-11}{0}$ part and instead write $z=11$, as follows:

$$
\frac{x-7}{-3}=\frac{y+9}{2},\,z=11
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Consider the straight line with the canonical equation $\dfrac{x}{5}=\dfrac{y+3}{3}=\dfrac{z-2}{1}.$ Find the vector equation of the line.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ and is parallel to the vector $\mathbf{v}=\langle v_x, v_y, v_z \rangle$ is given by

$$
\dfrac{x-x_0}{v_x}=\dfrac{y-y_0}{v_y}=\dfrac{z-z_0}{v_z} = t, \qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty).
$$

Comparing the above to our given equation

$$
\dfrac{x}{5}=\dfrac{y-(-3)}{3}=\dfrac{z-2}{1},
$$

we find that our line passes through the point $P(0,-3,2)$ and is parallel to $\mathbf{v}=\langle 5,3,1 \rangle.$ Therefore, its vector equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line Given in Parametric or Vector Form
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the straight line with the parametric equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1-2t \\ y=4t \\ z=-2+3t\end{aligned}
$$

for $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1-2t \\ 4t \\ -2+3t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2t \\ 4t \\ 3t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$

This implies that the given line passes through the point $P(1,0,-2)$ and is parallel to the vector $\mathbf{v}=\langle -2, 4, 3 \rangle.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\dfrac{x-1}{-2}=\dfrac{y}{4}=\dfrac{z-(-2)}{3} = t, 	\qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\dfrac{x-1}{-2}=\dfrac{y}{4}=\dfrac{z+2}{3}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line When a Component of the Direction Vector is Zero
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14083592/assets/4b3aa22ba1342c45d422c227258837ae080ee705f2580437c775bd2beaf8afeb.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\dfrac{x-1}{4}=\dfrac{y-2}{0}=\dfrac{z-3}{5} = t,	\qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\dfrac{x-1}{4}=\dfrac{y-2}{0}=\dfrac{z-3}{5},
$$

which is problematic because $\dfrac{y-2}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $y$ component always maintains the constant value of $y=2\mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14083592/assets/cafe7ac2b6224a50a288cabf6b6838c6a85a722404c9ebd20238f689f196b841.png)

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\dfrac{y-2}{0}$ part and instead write $y=2,$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{x-1}{4}=\dfrac{z-3}{5}, \; y=2
$$
